newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka pushes ahead with constitutional reform.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka pushes ahead with constitutional reform.

text.p: Sri Lanka on Wednesday released sections of a draft constitution that offers wide autonomy to minorities and aims to end the country's costly 13-year-old war with Tamil rebels.

Justice and Constitutional Affairs Minister Gamini Lakshman Peiris said 18 chapters of the draft constitution were being released, but a key chapter on devolution of power was held back as it was being debated by a parliamentary select committee.

"We will, within the next few weeks, complete the proposals with regards to devolution of power and the new constitutional package as a whole will be placed before parliament within the next couple of months," Peiris told a news conference.

The reforms aim to grant more autonomy to minorities and end the war with Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam rebels, whose struggle for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in the island's north and east has killed more than 50,000 people, according to government figures.
The new constitution proposes to abolish the country's executive presidency and the return to a parliamentary system.
Under the current system the president has huge powers, but the new constitution will vest all powers in the prime minister and make the president a ceremonial head of state.
It envisages the creation of several regional councils that would turn Sri Lanka into a federal state in all but name.

The chapters published on Wednesday, after 15 months of deliberation by the select committee, show a strengthening of fundamental rights, provision of judicial review of the legislature and strengthening of parliament, Peiris said.
"Another aspect of making democratic government of immediate benefit to the people is the initiative to devolve power to the proposed regional councils," a synopsis of the constitution said.
"This empowerment of people at the periphery will enable them to make decisions on issues directly relevant to them without reference to a central authority," the synopsis added.

The central government would have the power to take immediate measures, including the dissolution of a council, if any attempt was made by a regional council to secede or sever itself from the rest of Sri Lanka, it said.
The new constitution also introduces new guarantees for human rights and other freedoms.

"The constitutional changes that are reflected in the document are of a very far-reaching significance for the future of Sri Lanka," said Peiris, who is regarded as the architect of the new constitution.
He said last week's landslide victory for the ruling People's Alliance at local council elections strengthened the government's hand at taking the peace process forward.
The victory was seen as a puiblic endorsement of the government's peace proposals, originally announced in late 1995.

The government, which has only a one-vote majority in Sri Lanka's 225-seat parliament, needs the support of the main opposition United National Party to get the proposals passed by a two-thirds majority in the house.
If approved by parliament, the new constitution will be put to the people in a referendum.
